sentences.text: Dunhuangia is an extinct avialan genus belonging to the Enantiornithes clade, a group of medium-sized birds that lived in China during the Early Cretaceous.
The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — consists of a partial skeleton that lacks the skull but preserves the forelimbs, shoulder girdle, and sternum.

A unique feature of this bird is a pair of large notches on the rear edge of the sternum that equal over half the element's total length, while the coracoid bone features a deep trough on top bordered by a thick ridge.
The sternum possesses a pair of large notches on its rear edge that measure more than half the bone's total length.
Finding Enantiornithes in the coastal Changma Basin is unusual because these birds are typically arboreal.
The genus Dunhuangia was named and described in 2015 by Wang Min, Li Daqing, Jingmai Kathleen O'Connor, Zhou Zhonghe, and You Hailu, with the authority listed as Wang et al., 2015.
The generic name honors the city of Dunhuang in Gansu province, while the specific name of the type species, Dunhuangia junchangi, honors preparator Cui Guihia.
The holotype specimen GSGM-05-CM-030 was found in the Changma Basin within the Aptian-aged Xiagou Formation.
Within the Enantiornithes, Dunhuangia is classified as the sister species to Fortunguavis.
Dunhuangia lived between 121.4 and 113.2 million years ago during the Aptian stage in the area of present-day China.
